unit.title: Prepare vegetables, fruits, eggs and farinaceous dishes

summary: This unit teaches you to select, store, prepare and cook vegetables, ground provisions, fruit, eggs, rice, pasta, dumplings and other starchy (farinaceous) dishes, with Jamaican favourites such as ackee, callaloo, rice and peas, boiled dumplings, festival, cornmeal porridge and macaroni pie. You will also learn the food safety rules for each, how to hold and serve them, and how to cool, store and reheat them safely.

blocks.p: Vegetables, fruit, eggs and starchy foods make up most of what Jamaicans eat and a large part of every hotel and villa menu: breakfast eggs and fruit, vegetables and ground provisions with dinner, rice and peas on Sunday. They are cheap, healthy and popular, so a kitchen that cooks them well keeps guests happy and costs low. This unit is for HOSPITALITY VILLA/PROPERTIES SERVICES LEVEL 2 trainees.

Plain foods are not risk-free foods. Raw ackee that is not ripe is poisonous. Raw red kidney beans carry a toxin. Eggs can carry Salmonella. Cooked rice left warm grows bacteria that make poisons. So this unit teaches **safety and hygiene** alongside method.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and practical tasks in the Centre's training kitchen. In the practical tasks you prepare a vegetable plate and a fruit platter, cook rice and peas, dumplings and macaroni pie, and make egg dishes to order. The assessor watches your safety, hygiene, timing, tasting and clean-up as well as the finished plate.

blocks.h: Hygiene rules for fresh produce, eggs and starchy foods

ul: **Wash your hands** before you start, after handling raw eggs, soil-covered vegetables, waste or the toilet, and between jobs.
**Wash all fruit and vegetables** before peeling or cutting, to remove soil, insects and germs. Soil on a yam can carry bacteria that the knife spreads inside.
**Keep apart**: soil-covered produce and raw eggs away from ready-to-eat food, fruit and salads.
Use the **colour-coded boards** your Centre uses. A common code is green for salad and fruit, brown for root vegetables, red for raw meat and blue for raw fish; follow your Centre's code.
Do not use eggs for **raw or lightly cooked dishes** unless they are pasteurised.
Wash utensils and boards after raw eggs and after soil.
Cover cuts with a blue plaster and a glove.
Hold a Food Handler's Permit from the health department, as the law in Jamaica requires for food handlers.

head: Allergen or diet
Where it hides in this unit
What you do
rows: Eggs
Omelettes, pasta, batter, cakes, mayonnaise, macaroni pie
Check the recipe; tell the chef; use clean equipment
Wheat (gluten)
Dumplings, festival, pasta, bread, roux, spinners
Plain boiled yam, rice and plantain are naturally gluten-free, if nothing else is added
Milk
Cheese, butter, cream, milk in porridge and macaroni pie

Nuts and sesame
Some sauces, cakes and toppings
Check labels; wash boards and knives between foods
Vegetarian and vegan guests
Stock, saltfish, bacon and some beans seasoned with meat
Use vegetable stock; check the seasoning

blocks.note: If you are not sure whether a dish contains an allergen, **never guess**. Check the recipe and the labels, and ask the chef. A guest with a severe allergy can become seriously ill within minutes.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Vegetables give colour, flavour, fibre, vitamins and minerals. Good cooks keep as much of these as they can, by choosing fresh produce, storing it well and cooking it just enough.

head: Group
Examples
Notes
rows: Ground provisions (tubers and roots)
Yam, sweet potato, dasheen, coco, cassava, Irish potato
Starchy and filling; store cool and dry; Jamaican ground provisions are usually boiled, roasted or fried.
Leaf vegetables
Callaloo, cabbage, lettuce, pak choi, spinach
Wash very well; cook briefly; store in the fridge.
Fruit vegetables
Tomato, sweet pepper, cucumber, ackee, okra, cho cho, pumpkin, aubergine (garden egg)
Many are cooked as vegetables and used in sauces and stews.
Pod and seed vegetables
String beans, green peas, corn, gungo peas
Cook briefly; dried pulses need soaking.
Bulb and stem vegetables
Onion, scallion, garlic, celery, leek
Used for flavour in nearly everything.
Flower vegetables
Broccoli, cauliflower
Cook briefly; do not overcook.
Green fruit used as vegetables
Green banana, plantain, breadfruit
Starchy; boiled, roasted or fried.

ul: Check the **quantity** against the order and the **quality**: firm, bright and clean, with no bruises, mould, wilting, soft spots or insects.
Reject anything damaged, rotten or from an unknown source, and report it to your supervisor.
Check cold items arrive cold. Leafy vegetables and cut produce should be cool to the touch.
Put produce away promptly. Do not leave it in the sun on the loading bay.

head: Produce
How to store it
rows: Yam, sweet potato, Irish potato, dasheen, onion
A cool, dark, dry, airy place, off the floor, in crates or racks. Not in the fridge or freezer, and not in plastic bags. Light turns potatoes green.
Leafy vegetables (callaloo, lettuce, cabbage) and herbs
In the fridge, loosely covered or in a container, kept dry. Do not wash until needed.
Tomatoes
Ripen out of the fridge, then use quickly or chill.
Bananas, plantains, mangoes, pawpaw, avocado
Ripen at room temperature, away from direct sun. Chill when ripe if they must wait.
Cut fruit and vegetables
Covered, labelled and dated, in the fridge at 5 °C or below.
Dry goods (flour, rice, cornmeal, pasta, dried beans)
In sealed, labelled containers, in a cool, dry store, off the floor, away from pests.
Tinned goods
Cool, dry store; check for dents, rust and bulging; check the date.

ul: Use stock in order: **first in, first out**. Label with the date it arrived.
Check stock every day and throw away what has gone bad, so that it does not spoil the rest.
Keep soil-covered produce away from ready-to-eat food.

blocks.note: Irish potatoes that have turned green in parts contain a natural poison (solanine). Cut away the green parts deeply, or throw the potato away. Boiling does not remove it.
blocks.label: Safety

flow: Wash well in clean cold water
Trim and peel only what the recipe says, thinly
Cut to the right size and shape with a sharp knife
Keep cut vegetables covered, and in cold water if they brown (potato, yam)
Cook soon after cutting

ul: Peel thinly: much of the goodness lies just under the skin.
Cut to even sizes so that all pieces cook in the same time.
Do not soak vegetables for a long time: vitamins dissolve into the water.
Cut and cook as close to service as you can: vitamin C is lost as cut vegetables stand.
Use clean trimmings (onion and carrot ends, celery leaves) for vegetable stock.

head: Method
How it works
Good for
Points to remember
rows: Boiling
Cook in plenty of boiling water (salted).
Ground provisions, green banana, cabbage, string beans, carrots
Green vegetables go into **boiling** water and cook uncovered and briefly. Root vegetables may start in cold water.
Steaming
Cook over boiling water, with the food not touching the water.
Callaloo, cabbage, carrots, cho cho, broccoli, fish
Keeps colour, flavour and vitamins. Do not crowd the steamer.
Blanching and refreshing
Boil for a short time, then cool at once in iced water.
String beans, broccoli, tomatoes (for peeling)
Sets the colour; used when cooking ahead. Drain and chill, then reheat briefly.
Stir-frying
Cook small pieces fast in a little hot oil, stirring all the time.
Cabbage, carrots, peppers, string beans, callaloo
Cut to the same size, heat the pan first, do not overcrowd.
Shallow and deep frying
Cook in hot fat.
Plantain, yam, breadfruit chips, potato
Dry the food first; lay it away from you into the oil. Oil at about 160 to 180 °C for deep frying.
Roasting and baking
Cook with dry heat in the oven.
Breadfruit, pumpkin, sweet potato, potato, plantain
Cut to even sizes; oil lightly; turn them; roast hot, at about 180 to 220 °C.
Braising and stewing
Cook slowly in a little liquid, with a lid.
Cabbage, okra, pumpkin, cho cho
Low heat, covered; the liquid becomes the sauce.

ul: Cook green vegetables **quickly**, in plenty of boiling water, and uncovered, until just tender. Long cooking turns them grey and dull because the acids released turn the green pigment to brown.
**Do not add bicarbonate of soda** to keep colour: it destroys vitamin C and makes the vegetable soft and soapy.
Cook in **small batches** close to service. Do not keep cooked vegetables in water or in a hot cupboard for hours.
Use as little water as you can for vitamins that dissolve (vitamin C and the B vitamins). Use the cooking water for soups or sauces when it suits.
Do not overcook. 'Just tender' means the point of a knife goes in with a little resistance, and the vegetable keeps some bite.
Salt the water for boiled vegetables at the start, as the recipe says.

head: Fault
Likely cause
How to prevent it
rows: Grey, dull green vegetables
Overcooked; kept hot too long; cooked with the lid on
Cook fast, uncovered; serve at once; blanch and refresh if cooking ahead.
Soggy, mushy vegetables
Overcooked; pieces of different sizes; kept in water
Even sizes; test often; drain well; cook in small batches.
Hard, raw centres
Pieces too big or uneven; heat too high on the outside
Cut evenly; adjust the heat.
Potatoes or yam gone grey or brown after cutting
Left cut in the air
Keep in cold water until cooking.
Greasy fried food
Oil not hot enough; too much food at once
Heat the oil fully (about 160 to 180 °C); fry in small batches; drain on paper.
Burnt food in the oven
Heat too high; not turned
Check the temperature; turn the pieces.

sections.title: Jamaican vegetables, ground provisions and ackee

blocks.p: Ackee is Jamaica's national fruit and, with saltfish, makes the national dish. It is also a food that can **kill if it is wrongly prepared**. Unripe ackee contains a natural poison (hypoglycin) that causes severe vomiting, low blood sugar and, in some cases, death. This is sometimes called 'Jamaican vomiting sickness'.

head: Rule
Why
rows: Use only ackee from pods that have opened naturally on the tree
The yellow flesh (aril) is safe only when the fruit is fully ripe and the pod has opened by itself. Never force open a closed pod.
Take out and throw away the black seeds and the pink or red membrane
The seeds are poisonous, and the membrane (where the flesh joins the seed) holds much of the poison.
Use only the creamy yellow flesh; wash it
Removes any remains of membrane and dirt.
Boil the flesh in water until just tender; throw the water away
Cooking and discarding the water is the usual practice. Do not use the cooking water.
Never eat or use ackee from pods that are still closed, or fruit that is over-ripe, damaged or bad
The poison is highest in unripe fruit.
Buy canned ackee only from approved producers, in sound cans
Cans from approved producers are tested for safety.

ul: To make ackee and saltfish: soak or boil the saltfish to remove the salt, flake it and remove all skin and bones. Fry onion, scallion, tomato, sweet pepper, thyme and a little Scotch bonnet in oil. Add the saltfish, then fold in the cooked ackee **gently**, because it breaks up easily if stirred hard.
Serve hot with fried dumpling, festival, boiled green banana, yam, breadfruit or bammy, as the menu says.
Raw saltfish and boards that touched it must be cleaned and sanitised before ready-to-eat food is cut on them.

blocks.note: If you are unsure whether ackee is ripe, safe or properly prepared, do not use it. Ask your supervisor. Tell guests who ask that ackee is cooked and checked by the kitchen.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.h: Ground provisions, green banana and plantain

head: Item
How it is prepared
Notes
rows: Yam (Yellow yam, negro yam, white yam)
Wash; peel with a sharp knife; cut a flat base; cut into even pieces; boil in salted water until a knife goes in easily.
Do not overcook, or it falls apart. Slippery when raw: grip with a cloth.
Sweet potato
Wash, peel (or boil in the skin), cut and boil, roast or bake.
Cook until soft; goes sweet when roasted.
Dasheen and coco
Wash, peel (wear gloves if your skin itches), cut and boil.
Must be cooked well; raw they can irritate the mouth.
Green banana
Wash; cut the ends; slit the skin along its length; boil in the skin in salted water until the flesh is tender; then peel.
The sap stains hands and clothes black: oil your hands. Peel after boiling.
Plantain: green
Peel, slice and fry as chips, or boil.
Starchy and firm.
Plantain: ripe
Peel, slice on a slant and shallow fry until golden brown.
A yellow skin with black patches means sweet and ripe. Drain on kitchen paper.
Breadfruit
Roast whole in an oven or in coals, then peel, cut and serve; or peel, boil or fry.
Roasted breadfruit is a Jamaican favourite with ackee and saltfish.
Cassava (bammy)
Bammy is made from bitter cassava that has been grated and pressed to remove its poisonous juice, then baked or fried.
Never eat raw cassava. Buy bammy from a trusted source.
Cho cho (chayote)
Wash, peel under water if the sap irritates, halve, remove the seed, and boil, steam or stew.
Mild; takes on other flavours.
Pumpkin
Wash, cut, remove seeds and skin, cut evenly and boil, steam or add to soup.
Hard to cut: cut with the flat side down.

flow: Wash the callaloo several times in clean water, to remove soil and sand
Strip the leaves from the thick stems; chop the stems small if you use them
Chop or shred the leaves
Sweat onion, scallion, garlic, tomato and thyme in a little oil
Add the callaloo and steam it covered, over a gentle heat, for about 10 to 15 minutes until soft
Season, and serve hot

blocks.note: Callaloo cooks down to a small amount. Plan the portions: a large bundle may give only a few servings.
blocks.label: Tip

flow: Mix flour with a pinch of salt; add cold water a little at a time until a firm dough forms
Knead the dough until smooth, and rest it for a few minutes
Divide it into equal pieces and roll them into ovals or balls
Drop them into boiling, salted water and boil for about 15 to 20 minutes
They are done when they float and feel firm all through
Drain well away from your body and serve hot

blocks.p: Fruit is served fresh at breakfast and on platters, in drinks and in desserts. Because most fruit is eaten raw, it must be **clean, safe and fresh**.

ul: Wash your hands, and wash all fruit well, even fruit that will be peeled.
Use a clean **green** board (or the Centre's code for fruit) and a clean, sharp knife that has not touched raw meat or fish.
Peel, core and de-seed as the type needs, and cut to even sizes.
Slow **browning** (apple, banana, avocado, pear) by squeezing lime or lemon juice over the cut surface; acid slows the reaction with the air.
Cut fruit just before it is needed, or cover it and keep it at 5 °C or below.
Do not leave a cut fruit platter on a warm buffet for hours. Replace it with a fresh one.

head: Fruit
How to prepare it
rows: Pineapple
Wash; cut off the top and base so it stands flat; slice off the skin from top to bottom; take out the eyes; quarter, remove the core and slice.
Mango
Cut the two 'cheeks' off either side of the flat stone; score the flesh in a grid; turn the skin inside out or cut the flesh away.
Pawpaw (papaya)
Peel, halve, scoop out the seeds, cut into wedges or cubes.
Watermelon
Cut off the ends, halve, cut into wedges or cut off the rind and cube the flesh.
Orange and grapefruit
Cut off the peel and pith; cut out segments between the membranes.
Banana
Peel just before serving; brush with lime juice.
Soursop
Peel and take out the seeds; blend or strain the pulp for juice.
Avocado (pear)
Halve round the stone, twist, remove the stone, scoop or slice; squeeze lime juice on it.

flow: Wash your hands and all the fruit
Choose ripe, sound fruit of different colours
Prepare each kind on a clean board with a clean knife
Cut to even sizes; treat browning fruit with lime juice
Arrange the fruit neatly on a clean platter, with colours spaced out
Cover and chill at 5 °C or below until service
Garnish just before serving and keep the time out of the fridge short

blocks.note: A fruit platter looks best when the pieces are neat, the colours are mixed, nothing is bruised or brown, and the platter is not crowded. Guests eat with their eyes first.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: **Stewing**: simmer fruit gently in a little water and sugar until soft (apple, guava, ripe mango).
**Frying**: ripe plantain is fried in shallow oil until golden.
**Baking**: ripe plantain and bananas can be baked with a little butter and spices.
**Juices and drinks**: use clean equipment and safe water; keep chilled; serve the same day.

blocks.note: Jamaican fruits you may use include mango, pineapple, pawpaw, ackee, otaheite apple, star apple, guava, soursop, sweetsop, naseberry, June plum, watermelon, banana, plantain and citrus. Choose what is in season: it is fresher, tastier and cheaper.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Eggs are cheap, nourishing and useful for breakfast dishes, baking and sauces. They can carry **Salmonella** bacteria, on the shell and inside, so they need careful handling.

ul: **Shell**: hard but porous, and easily cracked. It can carry bacteria and soil.
**White (albumen)**: clear protein that sets white when cooked; whips into a foam.
**Yolk**: the yellow centre, rich in fat, vitamins and colour; it sets more slowly than the white.
**Air cell**: an air space at the blunt end that gets larger as the egg ages.

head: Test
Fresh egg
Old egg
rows: Water test (cold water in a bowl)
Sinks and lies flat
Stands up on its end, or floats (very old: do not use)
Cracked onto a plate
Yolk is round and high; thick white stays close around it
Yolk is flat; the white is thin and spreads out
Smell
No smell
A sulphur (rotten egg) smell: throw it away

ul: On delivery, check that shells are clean and **not cracked**, and that the date is in good order. Reject cracked or dirty eggs.
Store eggs in the **fridge**, in their tray, **away from strong smells** (eggshells absorb odours), and below ready-to-eat foods. Use first in, first out.
Take out only the amount you need. Do not wash eggs before storing.
Crack each egg into a **separate small bowl** before adding it to a mixture, so a bad egg or a piece of shell can be found without spoiling the rest.
Wash your hands after touching raw eggs and shells, and clean the board and the area.
Use **pasteurised egg** for dishes that are not cooked, such as fresh mayonnaise, mousses and some sauces; pasteurised egg is heat-treated to kill Salmonella.
Cook eggs fully for the very young, the elderly, pregnant women and those who are ill.
Do not keep egg dishes warm for hours. Egg mixtures, such as quiche and egg salad, must be chilled.

head: Method
How
Result and notes
rows: Boiled
Lower eggs into boiling water gently. Soft: about 3 to 4 minutes. Medium: about 5 to 6 minutes. Hard: about 10 to 12 minutes (times for a medium egg).
Cool hard-boiled eggs at once in cold water. This stops a **dark ring** (iron sulphide) forming round the yolk, and makes them easier to peel.
Poached

Bring water to a gentle simmer in a wide pan, with a splash of vinegar. Crack the egg into a cup, slide it in, and cook for about 3 to 4 minutes until the white is set and the yolk is soft. Lift out with a slotted spoon, drain and trim.
The vinegar helps the white set in a neat shape. Boiling hard breaks the egg up. Use very fresh eggs.
Fried
Heat a little oil or butter in a pan; crack in the egg; cook until the white is set. For sunny side up, do not turn. For over easy, turn once.
The pan must be hot enough but not smoking. Season at the end.
Scrambled
Beat eggs with salt and pepper (and a little milk if the recipe says). Cook over gentle heat, stirring all the time, until just set but still soft and creamy.
Take off the heat while still a little soft: they carry on cooking. High heat makes them hard and watery.
Omelette

Beat 2 or 3 eggs with seasoning. Pour into a hot, lightly buttered omelette pan. Stir with a fork and shake the pan, then stop. Put the filling in the middle, fold over and turn out onto a warm plate.
Quick, about 1 to 2 minutes. Lightly set, pale and neat (not browned, unless the recipe says).
Baked and in dishes
In quiches, custards and macaroni pie, eggs set the mixture in the oven.
Bake at a moderate heat until just set; a knife comes out clean.

flow: Cook the callaloo with onion, tomato and thyme, and keep it warm
Crack the eggs into a bowl, check them and beat with salt and pepper
Heat the pan, add a little butter, and pour in the eggs
Stir briefly, let them set, and add the callaloo
Fold over and turn onto a warm plate; serve at once

head: Fault
Cause
Prevention
rows: Dark ring round the yolk
Overcooked, and not cooled
Boil for the right time and cool at once in cold water.
Rubbery or dry scrambled eggs
Too hot or overcooked
Gentle heat; take off while still soft.
Poached egg spreads in the water
Old egg or boiling water
Use fresh eggs and a gentle simmer; a little vinegar.
Omelette is brown, tough or breaks
Pan too hot, too long, too many eggs
Moderate heat, 2 to 3 eggs, 1 to 2 minutes.
Shell in the mixture
Cracked straight in
Crack into a bowl first.

sections.title: Farinaceous dishes: rice, pasta, dumplings and cornmeal

blocks.p: **Farinaceous** (from the Latin word for flour) means dishes made mainly from starchy foods: rice, pasta, flour, cornmeal and similar grains. They are cheap, filling and popular, and nearly every Jamaican meal has one.

head: Method
How
Notes
rows: Absorption (steamed)

Measure the rice and water (about 1 part long-grain rice to 1.5 to 2 parts water, as the recipe says). Wash the rice, bring it to the boil with salt, cover and cook gently on low heat until all the water is absorbed. Rest for 5 to 10 minutes, then fluff with a fork.
Do not lift the lid or stir. Do not drain. Burnt rice means the heat was too high.
Boiled (plenty of water)
Boil rice in plenty of salted water until tender, drain and rinse.
Good for rice salads.

blocks.p: 'Peas' in Jamaica are red kidney beans or gungo peas, and **coconut milk** gives the dish its rich flavour.

flow: Pick over and wash the dried beans; soak overnight; **throw the soaking water away**
Boil the beans hard in fresh water for at least 10 minutes, then simmer until soft
Add coconut milk, garlic, thyme, scallion, pimento, a whole unburst Scotch bonnet and salt
Bring to a simmer; measure the liquid and add the washed rice
Cover and cook on low heat until the liquid is absorbed and the rice is tender
Remove the pepper and herb stalks; fluff with a fork and serve hot

blocks.note: Raw and undercooked dried red kidney beans contain a natural toxin that causes severe vomiting and diarrhoea. They must be soaked, the water thrown away, and then boiled hard for at least 10 minutes before simmering. Never use a slow cooker or low heat alone. Gungo peas and other dried pulses should also be cooked until soft.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: Keep the Scotch bonnet whole. If it bursts the rice will be very hot, and someone may be burned by a piece of it. Take it out before serving.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.h: Cooked rice: a food safety risk

blocks.p: Rice can carry spores of a bacterium (Bacillus cereus) that survive cooking. If cooked rice is left warm, the spores grow and make a toxin that **reheating does not destroy**. This causes vomiting and diarrhoea. The rule is: serve it hot or cool it fast.

ul: Serve rice hot, at about 63 °C or above, or cool it quickly.
Spread rice in a thin layer in a **shallow tray** to cool, then cover and chill at 5 °C or below within 1 to 2 hours, as your Centre's plan says.
Label and date the tray, and use it within the time the plan allows (often 1 day).
Reheat once, until steaming hot (about 74 °C in the centre), and throw away the rest.
Never keep rice at room temperature, in a rice cooker left on the 'off' setting, or on a bench for hours.

flow: Boil plenty of water (about 1 litre for each 100 g of pasta) and add salt
Add the pasta and stir at once, and now and then, so it does not stick
Cook, tasting before the packet time, until **al dente**: cooked but still a little firm to the bite
Drain well in a colander, pouring away from your body
Toss with the sauce or a little oil and serve at once

ul: Dried pasta: about 60 to 80 g a portion as a starter and 100 g or more as a main course.
Fresh pasta cooks in 2 to 3 minutes.
Do not rinse pasta that is to be served hot, because it washes away starch that helps the sauce cling. Rinse only for cold dishes.
To hold cooked pasta for later, cool it fast under cold water, drain, toss it in a little oil, cover and refrigerate; reheat in boiling water until piping hot.

flow: Boil the macaroni in salted water until just tender, and drain
Make a cheese mixture of grated cheese, milk, beaten egg, a little butter, mustard and seasoning
Mix with the macaroni and put into a greased baking dish
Top with cheese and bake at about 180 °C until golden and hot all through
Rest for a few minutes, cut into portions and serve hot

blocks.note: Macaroni is boiled only until just tender because it carries on cooking in the oven. If it is fully cooked first, the pie will be mushy.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Dish
Made from
How it is made
rows: Boiled dumplings
Flour, salt, water
Knead into a firm dough, shape, and boil for 15 to 20 minutes until firm and floating.
Fried dumplings
Flour, salt, baking powder, water
A softer dough, shaped and fried in shallow oil until golden; drain well.
Festival
Flour, cornmeal, sugar, salt, baking powder, butter or margarine, milk or water, vanilla
Mix into a dough, shape into long rolls, rest and fry in medium-hot oil until golden. Often served with fried fish.
Spinners
Flour and water
Rolled into thin lengths and dropped in soup to cook.
Cornmeal porridge
Cornmeal, water, milk, sugar, nutmeg, cinnamon, vanilla, a pinch of salt

Mix the cornmeal with **cold water first** to a smooth paste. Add it slowly to boiling water, stirring all the time, then simmer for about 15 to 20 minutes until thick and cooked. Add milk and flavourings.
Bammy
Cassava, salt
Made from pressed, grated bitter cassava, baked or fried; served with fish.

ul: **To stop lumps in cornmeal porridge**: mix the meal with cold water first, add it slowly to the hot liquid, and stir all the time.
**Dumpling dough** must rest so the gluten relaxes, or the dumplings will be tough.
Fry festival at about 170 to 180 °C so that it cooks through before it browns.
Drain fried food on kitchen paper.
**Taste with a clean spoon every time**, and put the used spoon in the wash-up. Never put a used spoon back in the pot.
Season in small amounts, and taste again after it has mixed in.
Jamaican seasoning includes thyme, scallion, garlic, pimento, Scotch bonnet pepper, onion and black pepper. Use as the standard recipe says: the flavour should match every time.
Add salt carefully: you can add more, but you cannot take it out.

blocks.p: A **standard recipe** gives the exact ingredients, weights, method and portion size. Following it keeps the taste, look and cost of the dish the same every time. To work out the amount for more portions, divide by the number the recipe makes and multiply by the number you need.

head: Example
Working
rows: A rice and peas recipe makes 10 portions and uses 800 g rice. How much rice for 40 portions?
40 ÷ 10 = 4 times the recipe; 800 g × 4 = 3200 g = 3.2 kg.
A tray of macaroni pie is cut into 12 portions. How many trays for 60 guests?

ul: Serve hot food **hot**, on warm plates, and cold food cold. A cold plate takes the heat out of the food.
Hot-hold at about 63 °C or above, in a hot cupboard or bain-marie; check with a clean probe.
Cook vegetables in small batches close to service, to keep colour and texture.
Plate neatly: put the starch, vegetable and main item in clear places; do not let sauce run over the rim; wipe the rim clean.
Garnish simply: a herb sprig, a wedge of lime, a few slices of tomato or cucumber.
Never put used food back into the serving pot.
Cool rice and cooked starchy foods fast in shallow trays, then cover, label, date and chill at 5 °C or below.
Reheat once only, until steaming hot (about 74 °C in the centre), and throw away what is left.
Store cut fruit and vegetables covered at 5 °C or below.
Do not reuse cooking oil that is dark, smells, or smokes.
Peel thinly and trim carefully. Weigh trimmings to see the waste.
Save clean trimmings for vegetable stock. Compost or bin the rest.
Use ripe fruit first; use bruised fruit for juices, stewing or baking.
Cook only what you need. Plan the quantity from the number of covers.
Clean and sanitise boards, knives, pots, pans, peelers and surfaces; dry them.
Switch off, unplug and clean the food processor; the blades are sharp.
Strain used cooking oil, let it cool and store or throw it away as your Centre says; never pour it down the sink.
Wipe the stove, sweep and mop the floor; take rubbish out.
Wash your hands and record temperatures on the temperature log.

Starchy roots and tubers such as yam, coco, dasheen, sweet potato and green banana.
Jamaica's national fruit; safe only when ripe and the pod has opened naturally, with seeds and membrane removed.
The natural poison in unripe ackee.
A leafy green vegetable, steamed with onion, tomato and thyme.
To boil briefly and then cool at once in iced water.
To cool food in cold or iced water after cooking.

Egg that has been heat-treated to kill bacteria, for uncooked dishes.
To cook gently in liquid that is just simmering.
Cooked but still slightly firm to the bite.

c1.title: Ackee season at a hotel in Port Maria
c1.text: It is ackee season, and a supplier delivers a large basket of fresh ackee to a hotel kitchen in Port Maria. Trainee Rohan finds that some of the pods are fully open, and some are still closed with the red pod just starting to split. His colleague says, 'Just pull the closed ones open, they are fine.' Rohan is told to prepare the ackee for breakfast, and he plans to boil the yellow flesh and use the water for the sauce.

c2.title: Breakfast eggs at a villa in Negril
c2.text: At a villa in Negril, the guests of a family from Canada order a poached egg, a callaloo omelette and a hard-boiled egg for a child. Chef Tanya has stored the eggs in a bowl on the counter beside the stove. Trainee Janelle cracks six eggs together into the beating bowl, finds a shell piece and then has to throw all of them away. The hard-boiled egg she serves has a dark-green ring around the yolk, and the poached egg has spread out into thin strands in the water.

c3.title: Rice and peas for a school function in Spanish Town
c3.text: A school in Spanish Town orders rice and peas for 120 students. The kitchen cooks the rice at 8 a.m. and leaves it in a big covered pot on the counter until lunch at 1 p.m. The cook had used red kidney beans soaked overnight, but he cooked them in the same water and simmered them gently for 30 minutes. The rice is partly mushy and partly hard.

c4.title: A vegetable plate for a banquet in Kingston
c4.text: A hotel in Kingston is serving a vegetable plate of steamed cabbage, string beans, carrots and boiled yam to 80 guests. The string beans were boiled with the lid on for 25 minutes, and they have turned a dull olive-grey. Trainee Marlon peeled and cut the Irish potatoes two hours early and left them on the bench, and they have turned grey-brown. He has put a sack of yams in the fridge.

c5.title: Pasta lunch at a cook shop in Montego Bay
c5.text: A small cook shop in Montego Bay serves a pasta lunch to 40 customers. Trainee Kimberly boils 4 kg of macaroni in a medium pot with a little water, and stirs it only at the end. It sticks together, and some of it is soft and some hard. She plans to bake it as macaroni pie, so she cooks it fully first.

questions.q: What should Rohan do about the pods that are still closed?
o: Open them by hand when the flesh looks yellow enough
Boil them whole, and throw the pods away afterwards
Leave them, and use only fruit from pods that opened naturally
Cook them for longer than the open ones to make them safe
questions.why: Ackee is safe only when it has ripened and the pod has opened by itself on the tree. Forcing a pod open, or cooking unripe fruit longer, does not make it safe.

questions.q: What must be removed from the opened ackee before cooking?
o: The black seeds and the pink-red membrane
The yellow flesh, which is hard to digest
Only the pod, because the flesh has no waste
The thin outer skin of the yellow flesh
questions.why: The black seeds and the membrane that joins the flesh to the seed hold the poison. Only the creamy yellow flesh is used.

questions.q: Rohan plans to use the water from boiling the ackee in the sauce. Why is this wrong?
o: The water is too weak to give any flavour to a sauce
The water would make the sauce too thin and watery
The water turns the saltfish a different colour in the pot
The water should be thrown away, as it may carry the poison
questions.why: The usual practice is to boil the ackee and throw the water away, because any poison that has come out of the fruit is left in it.

questions.q: How should the cooked ackee be added to the saltfish?
o: Stir it in hard so that it mixes through the fish at once
Fold it in gently, as it breaks up easily
Add it first, then fry the saltfish and onions on top
Mash it into a paste before it goes in the pan
questions.why: Cooked ackee is soft and breaks up easily; fold it in gently at the end so that the pieces stay whole.

questions.q: Where should Chef Tanya store the eggs?
o: In a bowl on the counter, so they stay at room temperature
In the fridge, in their tray, away from strong smells
In a cool dry store beside the rice and flour
In the freezer in their shells, so they keep for longer
questions.why: Eggs are kept in the fridge to slow bacteria such as Salmonella, and away from strong smells because shells are porous. They should not be left beside a stove.

questions.q: After Janelle has cracked the raw eggs, what must she do before she goes on to the next dish?
o: Wipe her hands on her apron and carry on, since the eggs are in the bowl
Wash her hands, then clean and sanitise the bench and the bowl
Rinse her fingers under cold water, then dry them on a side towel
Put on a new apron, and leave the bench until the end of service
questions.why: Raw egg and shell can carry Salmonella. Wash your hands and clean and sanitise the area, so that the germs are not carried to other food.

questions.q: What caused the dark ring around the yolk of the hard-boiled egg?
o: The egg was too fresh when it was boiled
The water was not salted well enough
The egg was kept in the fridge for too long
It was overcooked and not cooled at once in cold water
questions.why: A green-grey ring forms when an egg is boiled too long, and especially when it is not cooled quickly. Boil for the time given and cool it straight away.

questions.q: How should Janelle poach the egg so that it keeps its shape?
o: Use a very fresh egg in water that is barely simmering, with a little vinegar
Boil the water hard and drop the egg in from a height
Use an old egg, which has a firmer white that holds together
Add salt to cold water and heat the egg slowly with the water
questions.why: A fresh egg has a thick white that holds together. Gentle simmering and a splash of vinegar help it set; hard boiling tears it into strands.

questions.q: What is the main risk from the rice being left on the counter for five hours?
o: It would go hard and dry, and the grains would split
It would lose its flavour as the coconut milk separates
Bacteria in it could produce toxins that reheating does not destroy
It would take in moisture from the air and turn sour at once
questions.why: Rice carries spores that survive cooking, and if the rice is left warm they grow and make a toxin that heat does not destroy. Serve rice hot or cool it fast in shallow trays and chill it.

questions.q: What is wrong with how the cook prepared the red kidney beans?
o: He should have used tinned beans in place of dried ones
He should have soaked them for at least a whole week
He should have added the salt before the beans started to boil
He should have drained them and boiled them hard in fresh water
questions.why: Red kidney beans contain a toxin. Soak them, throw the water away, boil hard in fresh water for at least 10 minutes, then simmer until soft. A gentle 30 minutes in the soaking water is not safe.

questions.q: The rice is partly mushy and partly hard. Which is the most likely cause?
o: The amount of water was not measured, and the heat was uneven
The rice was washed too well before it was cooked
The pot lid was kept on tightly for the whole time
The coconut milk was added at the very start of the cooking
questions.why: Absorption rice needs the right measure of liquid, a pot with a heavy base and an even low heat. Too much water in part of the pot gives mush, too little gives hard grains. Do not stir or lift the lid.

questions.q: Some of the rice is left over after lunch. It stood at room temperature from 8 a.m. What should be done with it?
o: Throw it away, because it has been in the danger zone for too long
Reheat it until steaming hot, and serve it again tomorrow
Spread it in a tray, chill it, and use it in fried rice tomorrow
Keep it covered in the pot, and reheat it in the bain-marie
questions.why: Rice left warm for hours may hold a toxin that reheating does not destroy. Food held in the danger zone for that long must be thrown away.

questions.q: Why did the string beans turn a dull olive-grey?
o: They were not washed well enough before they were cooked
They were cooked in too much water, so their colour washed out
They were cooked for too long and with the lid on
They were cut into pieces that were all of the same size
questions.why: Long cooking with the lid on keeps in the acids that turn the green pigment dull. Cook green vegetables quickly, in boiling water, uncovered, and serve at once.

questions.q: How should Marlon keep cut Irish potatoes from going grey-brown while they wait?
o: Spread them on a tray in the open air to dry
Cover them with a cloth on the bench
Keep them in cold water until they are cooked
Keep them in warm water so they stay soft
questions.why: Cut potato reacts with the air and browns. Cold water keeps the air away. Better still, cut them close to cooking time.

questions.q: What is wrong with putting the sack of yams in the fridge?
o: Yams should be kept in cool, dark, dry, airy storage, not in the fridge
Yams must always be kept in the freezer in sealed bags
Yams are best kept in a bowl of water in the sun
Yams need to be stored wet in a closed plastic bag
questions.why: Ground provisions keep best in a cool, dark, dry, airy place. Cold, damp or sealed storage makes them spoil.

questions.q: Marlon wants the string beans to keep their colour for 80 guests. What is the best plan?
o: Cook them all at once in the morning and hold them in hot water
Add a spoon of bicarbonate of soda to the cooking water
Boil them with the lid on, then keep them in a hot cupboard
Cook small batches in boiling water close to service
questions.why: Small, quick batches near service give the best colour and vitamins. Bicarbonate of soda destroys vitamin C and makes the beans soft, and long holding turns them dull.

questions.q: Why did Kimberly's pasta stick together?
o: She used too little water and did not stir it early on
She salted the water, which makes pasta stick
She boiled it too fast and drained it too soon
She used macaroni, which is too small for plenty of water
questions.why: Pasta needs plenty of boiling water and an early stir so the pieces do not clump together on the base of the pot. A guide is about 1 litre of water for 100 g of pasta.

questions.q: Why should the macaroni for a pie be boiled only until just tender?
o: Because it will go on cooking in the oven
Because the cheese needs a hard base to melt on
Because it will soak up the egg and turn rubbery
Because boiled macaroni cannot be baked until it is cold
questions.why: It finishes cooking in the hot cheese mixture in the oven. If it is fully cooked first, the pie ends up mushy.

questions.q: A cook mixes cornmeal straight into boiling water and it forms lumps. What should she have done?
o: Mixed the meal with cold water into a paste first and added it slowly, stirring
Added the cornmeal to cold milk, and boiled the whole pot hard
Cooked the cornmeal in a dry pan until it turned brown first
Added extra cornmeal, to soak up the lumps as they formed
questions.why: Dry cornmeal poured into boiling water cooks on the outside and forms lumps. A smooth paste made with cold water spreads evenly in the hot liquid.

questions.q: A recipe makes 10 portions of rice and peas from 800 g of rice. How much rice is needed for 60 portions?
o: 4.8 kg
6 kg
3.2 kg
8 kg
questions.why: 60 ÷ 10 = 6 times the recipe, so 800 g × 6 = 4800 g = 4.8 kg. Check it another way: 800 ÷ 10 = 80 g per portion, and 80 × 60 = 4800 g.
